::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## TL;DR

Warm air holds far more water vapour than cold air, and the relationship is exponential rather than linear. Clausius-Clapeyron says how steeply.
:::

## The saturation curve

Water vapor in the atmosphere is an invisible gas. For condensation to occur, the air must reach **saturation** ($100\%$ Relative Humidity), where the rate of water condensation equals the rate of evaporation.

The maximum amount of water vapor air can hold at equilibrium is the **saturation vapor pressure** $e_s(T)$, governed by the **Clausius-Clapeyron equation**:

$$\frac{d e_s}{d T} = \frac{L_v(T) \cdot e_s(T)}{R_v \cdot T^2}$$

Integrating this yields the exponential dependence of saturation on temperature:

$$e_s(T) \approx e_0 \cdot \exp\left( \frac{L_v}{R_v} \left( \frac{1}{T_0} - \frac{1}{T} \right) \right)$$

where:

- $L_v \approx 2.501 \times 10^6 \text{ J/kg}$ is the latent heat of vaporization.
- $R_v = 461.5 \text{ J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$ is the specific gas constant for water vapor.
- $e_0 \approx 6.11 \text{ hPa}$ at $T_0 = 273.15 \text{ K}$ ($0^\circ\text{C}$).

<figcaption><strong>Figure 1 | Air's capacity for water vapour rises exponentially with temperature, which is why cooling — not moistening — makes clouds.</strong> Integrating the Clausius-Clapeyron relation gives a saturation vapour pressure $e_s(T)$ that curves upward steeply: saturated air at $0^\circ\text{C}$ holds about $6\text{ hPa}$ of vapour, while at $30^\circ\text{C}$ it holds roughly $42\text{ hPa}$ — seven times more. Read the same slope backwards and every $1^\circ\text{C}$ of cooling removes about $7\%$ of the capacity. Because the shaded region under the curve is the only vapour the air can carry, a parcel pushed below the curve by a few hundred metres of lift must shed its surplus as liquid.</figcaption>
</figure>

## Key takeaways

- Air is saturated when condensation and evaporation balance; that ceiling is the saturation vapour pressure $e_s(T)$, and it depends on temperature alone.
- Clausius-Clapeyron makes $e_s$ exponential in temperature: saturated air at $30^\circ\text{C}$ holds about seven times the vapour of air at $0^\circ\text{C}$.
- For every $1^\circ\text{C}$ drop in air temperature, saturation vapor pressure drops by roughly $7\%$, so cooling air is the most efficient way to force vapour into liquid droplets.
- A parcel lifted a few hundred metres cools past the curve and has to shed its surplus vapour as liquid.
